explanation.text: fatherless--Our whole land is full of orphans [CALVIN]. Or, "we are fatherless," being abandoned by Thee our "Father" (Jer 3:19), [GROTIUS].

explanation.text:
water for money--The Jews were compelled to pay the enemy for the water of their own cisterns after the overthrow of Jerusalem; or rather, it refers to their sojourn in Babylon; they had to pay tax for access to the rivers and fountains. Thus, "our" means the water which we need, the commonest necessary of life.

our wood--In Judea each one could get wood without pay; in Babylon, "our wood," the wood we need, must be paid for.

bsb.text: We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price.

explanation.text: Literally, "On our necks we are persecuted"; that is, Men tread on our necks (Psa 66:12; Isa 51:23; compare Jos 10:24). The extremest oppression. The foe not merely galled the Jews face, back, and sides, but their neck. A just retribution, as they had been stiff in neck against the yoke of God (Ch2 30:8, Margin; Neh 9:29; Isa 48:4).

bsb.text: We are closely pursued; we are weary and find no rest.

explanation.text:

to . . . Egyptians--at the death of Josiah (Ch2 36:3-4).

Assyrians--that is, the Chaldeans who occupied the empire which Assyria had held. So Jer 2:18.

(Jer 31:29).

borne their iniquities--that is, the punishment of them. The accumulated sins of our fathers from age to age, as well as our own, are visited on us. They say this as a plea why God should pity them (compare Eze 18:2, etc.).

bsb.text: Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment.

explanation.text: Servants . . . ruled . . . us--Servants under the Chaldean governors ruled the Jews (Neh 5:15). Israel, once a "kingdom of priests" (Exo 19:6), is become like Canaan, "a servant of servants," according to the curse (Gen 9:25). The Chaldeans were designed to be "servants" of Shem, being descended from Ham (Gen 9:26). Now through the Jews' sin, their positions are reversed.

bsb.text: Slaves rule over us; there is no one to deliver us from their hands.

We gat our bread with . . . peril--that is, those of us left in the city after its capture by the Chaldeans.

because of . . . sword of . . . wilderness--because of the liability to attack by the robber Arabs of the wilderness, through which the Jews had to pass to get "bread" from Egypt (compare Lam 5:6).

bsb.text: We get our bread at the risk of our lives because of the sword in the wilderness.

explanation.text: As an oven is scorched with too much fire, so our skin with the hot blast of famine (Margin, rightly, "storms," like the hot simoom). Hunger dries up the pores so that the skin becomes like as if it were scorched by the sun (Job 30:30; Psa 119:83).

explanation.text: So in just retribution Babylon itself should fare in the end. Jerusalem shall for the last time suffer these woes before her final restoration (Zac 14:2).

explanation.text: Aged men in the East meet in the open space round the gate to decide judicial trials and to hold social converse (Job 29:7-8).

explanation.text:
The joy of our heart is ceased,.... ward joy was gone, as well as the external signs of it: it "sabbatized", as it may be rendered; alluding perhaps to the cordial joy expressed formerly on their sabbaths and other festivals, now not observed; at least, not with that joy, inward and outward, they formerly were:

our dance is turned into mourning; which also was used at their solemn feasts, as well as at their common diversions, Judges 21:21; but now no more of that; but, instead of it, mourning at the calamities they were oppressed with; and at the remembrance of mercies and privileges, civil and religious, they were deprived of.

explanation.text: (Psa 102:12). The perpetuity of God's rule over human affairs, however He may seem to let His people be oppressed for a time, is their ground of hope of restoration.

explanation.text: (Psa 80:3; Jer 31:18). "Restore us to favor with Thee, and so we shall be restored to our old position" [GROTIUS]. Jeremiah is not speaking of spiritual conversion, but of that outward turning whereby God receives men into His fatherly favor, manifested in bestowing prosperity [CALVIN]. Still, as Israel is a type of the Church, temporal goods typify spiritual blessings; and so the sinner may use this prayer for God to convert him.

bsb.text: Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old,

21.interlinear: Turn/H7725 thou us unto thee O LORD/H3068 and we shall be turned/H7725 renew/H2318 our days/H3117 as of old/H6924

explanation.text:
Rather, "Unless haply Thou hast utterly rejected us, and art beyond measure wroth against us," that is, Unless Thou art implacable, which is impossible, hear our prayer [CALVIN]. Or, as Margin, "For wouldest Thou utterly reject us?" etc.--No; that cannot be. The Jews, in this book, and in Isaiah and Malachi, to avoid the ill-omen of a mournful closing sentence, repeat the verse immediately preceding the last [CALVIN].
